flags.why: Text says this Nightjar was "the first ever captured or seen here, and sent to me", so it was in hand; 'caught' is more specific than 'seen'.

flags.right_value: thick haze, approaching to fog, with a continuous downpour of rain
flags.why: The text's weather runs on: "approaching to fog, with a continuous downpour of rain; wind S.E." The extractor dropped the rain.
The Gutenberg text has it too: "came from north, stopped on island." The extractor stopped the quote short; 'stopped on island' is settled.
"During the first two weeks of October Wild Ducks are reported as passing" is a general summary; "At Morecambe" belongs to the previous sentence.
"Great numbers of Larks ... from 2 to 5 a.m." is rightly 'seen'; "great numbers struck" is its own observation (as in Example 1), not a fix to this one.

The transcription reads "11.80
a.m." and the record copies it exactly; the print has 11.30.
From "mod. N. by E. breeze", wind is the bearing; the extractor splits force out elsewhere (67, 69).
"mod. N. by E. breeze": "mod." is the force and belongs in force, not lumped into wind.
"From the same station": "Skerries" appears in neither the chunk nor the given context, so null is right by the rules.
"caught at lighthouse": the rules separate the lighthouse from the lantern or light; neither the lantern nor the light is named.
"flying N.E. to land, 2 p.m., ... two young ones struck lantern": whether the entry's 2 p.m. also covers the striking is a reading of how far the time reaches.
"strong E.S.E. breeze": the wind is the bearing; "strong" goes in force.
"strong E.S.E. breeze": force is stated, so null is wrong.
"mod. W.N.W. gale": "mod." alone drops the gale, but "mod. gale" isn't an unbroken string in the text, so the rules allow either.
"fresh E.S.E. gale": "fresh gale" isn't an unbroken string in the text, and "fresh" alone drops the gale; same split problem as 67.
"fresh N. breeze": the wind is the bearing; "fresh" goes in force.
"fresh N. breeze": force is stated, so null is wrong.
"one killed, fresh E.S.E. breeze": force is "fresh" (and wind should be "E.S.E.").
"On one occasion a monster pie ... contained two hundred Larks" is a separate occasion; the text doesn't tie these Larks to the light.

"large flights of
Rooks rest here ... remain to be caught": the count is printed and is inside the quote.
"a few Sea Gulls each day": 'each day' is how often more than a time of day; either reading fits the rules.
